Nearly launched on September 22. In under 2 weeks:
$23M+ volume
2,400+ token launches
8,800 traders
$142K paid to creators
$196K of $NEARLY burned

More importantly, we are seeing new ecosystem runners emerge with thousands of holders and entirely new communities forming on NEAR.

We have shipped social trading, tokenized stocks, stock pairs, holder dividends, creator rewards, referrals, limit orders and buyback & burn.

And we are using protocol fees to grow the ecosystem further, rewarding builders and communities, supporting ecosystem tokens, rewarding holders and bringing more liquidity on-chain.

The goal with Nearly was never just to build another launchpad.

We want to create an ecosystem where new users come to NEAR, new communities are formed, builders have more ways to launch and grow and the value generated by the protocol flows back into the ecosystem.

This is what we have built in less than two weeks.

A lot more to ship!

Build in public is becoming almost impossible in AI.

There’s very little creativity in the space right now. The moment something works, everyone converges on it.

Jev launches, blows up, and within days you have clones everywhere. Within 2 weeks, major platforms are shipping their own versions of the same basic idea.

And this is only going to get worse because software itself is becoming cheap.

You can spend months designing and building something genuinely complex, show it publicly, and someone with good AI coding agents can reproduce 80% of it frighteningly fast.

Complexity used to be a moat. Increasingly, it isn’t.

The scarce thing now isn’t the ability to write the software. It’s having an idea worth copying in the first place, distribution, proprietary data, customer relationships, and the ability to keep moving after everyone copies you.

Building in public used to be marketing.

In AI, sometimes you’re just publishing free product research for your competitors.

My position on "MIA's illusion"
Honestly, I really liked how MIA's AI Lab pushed Local AI like crazy and built a strong community around an avatar. But too many things now overshadow the positives:
1 - Using open-source code with unclear or insufficient attribution to its creators.
2 - Taking reach away from everyone else working on AI, especially newer accounts with fewer followers who work hard to earn their audience's trust through real work and passion (see point 1).
3 - ☠️ Selling a book on how to grow on X. This was the worst move, and I really didn't like it. Using an avatar, building a community, growing your audience: all fine. But monetizing those tactics by selling them to the very community you built goes against the basic values a community should have.
4 - Now blocking anyone who criticizes the account or the way it operates. That's the opposite of an open community, where everyone has the right to say what they think, good or bad, for or against.

I hope you'll never see me do anything like this, and if I ever do, please tell me immediately. But I really doubt it, simply because:
- I love Local AI and AI in general. 
- I left my startup to go all-in on this world: to play with, study, and live every aspect of this revolution, and to be an active part of its community.
- I love tinkering with hardware and software: Apple, Nvidia, AMD, you name it.
- I'm financially independent, so I'm free to write, say, buy, and play with whatever I want, and I don't need to sell anything to anyone.

❗️ AMD's driver just outed the chips inside the PlayStation 6 and Steam Deck 2, after Adrenalin 26.9.2 shipped with three unreleased codenames called ATlite3, AT2 and Gainsborough.

ATlite3 is likely the PS6 GPU because the PS5's was called Navi10lite during development, leaker Kepler_L2 says.

Gainsborough may be the Steam Deck 2 chip, since Valve's earlier ones were codenamed Aerith and Sephiroth and Aerith's surname in Final Fantasy VII is Gainsborough.

Before he became Sergeant Stubby, he was simply a stray Staffordshire terrier mix who wandered onto a training field and found himself a soldier.

In 1917, Stubby befriended Private J. Robert Conroy while the 102nd Infantry was training in Connecticut. When the unit shipped overseas for World War I, Conroy brought his little companion along.

Stubby would go on to serve alongside American troops in France. He survived a gas attack and became sensitive enough to the danger that he later warned sleeping soldiers of another attack. He helped locate wounded men on the battlefield, alerted troops to danger, and even helped capture a German soldier near the Allied trenches.

During his service, Stubby participated in 17 battles and was wounded by shrapnel. His famous coat eventually carried medals and decorations commemorating the little dog who had shared the dangers of war alongside American soldiers.

Stubby returned home a hero.

But perhaps his greatest honor wasn't hanging from his coat.

It was the trust of the soldiers who slept beside him, fought beside him, and knew that when danger came, their little four-legged brother would be right there with them.

From a little stray Staffordshire terrier mix to Sergeant Stubby, his story has survived for more than a century.

Courage doesn't always wear a uniform.

Sometimes it walks beside one on four paws. 🇺🇸🐾❤️
